metadata.title: Forces Acting on Trust In Government
metadata.description: The full four-loop system. Two reinforcing loops (gerrymandering and disinformation) push trust down. Two balancing loops (civic reform and free-press accountability) push trust back up by reducing political corruption. Whether trust recovers or collapses depends on which set of loops dominates.
metadata.author: US Government Intelligent Textbook

nodes.label: Trust In Government
nodes.description: The central stock. The percentage of citizens who say they trust the federal government to do what is right most or all of the time. Every loop in this diagram flows through this node.

nodes.label: Partisan Hostility
nodes.description: How strongly members of one party see the other as illegitimate or dangerous.

nodes.label: Partisan Gerrymandering
nodes.description: Drawing district lines to favor one party. One side's aggressive map invites retaliation from the other.

nodes.label: Uncompetitive Elections
nodes.description: Safe seats where the outcome is decided by the map, not the voters.

nodes.label: Alternative Media Use
nodes.description: Reliance on partisan blogs, social media influencers, and conspiracy forums instead of mainstream journalism.

nodes.label: Disinformation Spread
nodes.description: False or misleading content circulating about elections, officials, and government programs.

nodes.label: Belief in Conspiracies
nodes.description: Belief that elections are rigged or that government is secretly controlled.

nodes.label: Civic Activism
nodes.description: Turnout, protest, organizing, and demand for reform candidates.

nodes.label: Anti-Corruption Reforms
nodes.description: Ethics laws, inspectors general, campaign finance disclosure, and lobbying restrictions.

nodes.label: Investigative Journalism
nodes.description: Press reporting that exposes hidden wrongdoing — enabled by the First Amendment.

nodes.label: Officials Held Accountable
nodes.description: Resignations, indictments, hearings, and electoral defeats that follow exposed wrongdoing.

nodes.label: Political Corruption
nodes.description: Bribery, self-dealing, and abuse of office. Shared by both balancing loops — reforms reduce it from one side, accountability reduces it from the other.

edges.description: Low trust in shared institutions makes the other party look like the threat.
Hostility justifies aggressive map-drawing as self-defense.
Safe seats are the direct output of partisan maps.
If your vote doesn't matter, trust falls.
When official sources lose credibility, citizens look elsewhere.
Weaker fact-checking lets falsehoods spread faster.
Repeated exposure to false claims makes them feel true.
If you believe the system is rigged, you cannot trust it.
Distrust mobilizes citizens to demand change.
Disclosure and oversight rules make corruption costlier.
Distrust drives demand and motivation for accountability reporting.
Exposed wrongdoing prompts prosecutors, hearings, and voters to act.
Real consequences for past offenders deter future ones.
Visible corruption drives trust down; reducing it lets trust recover. This single edge is shared by both balancing loops.

loops.label: R1: Gerrymandering Arms Race
loops.description: Distrust → hostility → gerrymandering → uncompetitive elections → more distrust.

loops.label: R2: Disinformation Spiral
loops.description: Distrust → alternative media → disinformation → conspiracies → more distrust.

loops.label: B1: Civic Reform Pressure
loops.description: Distrust → activism → reforms → less corruption → trust recovers.

loops.label: B2: Free Press Accountability
loops.description: Distrust → journalism → accountability → less corruption → trust recovers.

key_insights: Two reinforcing loops (R1, R2) drive trust down; two balancing loops (B1, B2) push it back up. The system's trajectory depends on which set is stronger at any given moment.
Political corruption sits at the bottom of the diagram as the shared variable — both balancing loops work by reducing it.
The Framers built B2 into the Constitution itself: the First Amendment makes investigative journalism legal even when it embarrasses the government.
discussion_questions: Which of the four loops do you think is strongest in the U.S. today? Use evidence to support your answer.
Pick one loop and identify a single intervention that would weaken it (if reinforcing) or strengthen it (if balancing).
Are there feedback loops missing from this diagram? Sketch one you would add.
